description: Terex Corporation manufactures industrial equipment for materials processing machinery, waste and recycling solutions, mobile elevating work platforms, and equipment for the electric utility industry
description_full: Terex Corporation manufactures industrial equipment for materials processing machinery, waste and recycling solutions, mobile elevating work platforms, and equipment for the electric utility industry worldwide. The MP segment offers crushers, washing systems, screens, trommels, apron feeders, material handlers, pick and carry cranes, wood processing, biomass and recycling equipment, concrete mixer trucks and concrete pavers, conveyors, and replacement parts under the Terex, Powerscreen, Fuchs, EvoQuip, Canica, Cedarapids, CBI, Simplicity, Franna, Terex Ecotec, Finlay, ProAll, ZenRobotics, Terex Washing Systems, Terex MPS, Terex Jaques, Advance, Bid-Well, MDS, MARCO, MAGNA, Green-Tec, and Terex Recycling Systems brands. Its products are used in construction, infrastructure, and recycling projects; quarrying, mining, and material handling applications; maintenance applications to lift equipment or material; and landscaping and biomass production industries. The Aerials segment provides aerial work platform equipment, and telehandlers under the Terex and Genie brands; and portable material lifts, portable aerial work platforms, trailer-mounted articulating booms, self-propelled articulating and telescopic booms, and scissor lifts for construction and maintenance of industrial, commercial, institutional, and residential buildings and facilities, commercial operations, and tree trimming and various infrastructure projects. The ES segments offers refuse collection bodies, hydraulic cart lifters, automated carry cans, utility equipment, compaction, balers, recycling equipment, diggers derricks, transmission and distribution lines, construction and foundation drilling applications, insulated aerial devices, and cameras under the Heil, Marathon, 3rd Eye, Soft-Pak, Connected Collections, Parts Central, Curotto-Can, and Bayne Thinline brands; and waste hauler software solutions. The company was founded in 1933 and is based in Norwalk, Connecticut.

Each employee generates $30K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $3K per employee reflects an ownership culture. financial_summary: Terex Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $6.4B market cap on $5.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and -2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 9% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 19% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $322M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.99× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 9% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.79x).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+31.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 13% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 24% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 48% and a beta of 1.25, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.50 vs 5y 1.36), so read it loosely.
About $67.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 90% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 26% below its DCF fair value of $76.83, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 48%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $55.45 to $107 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 25% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 5.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $74.35 on average, 31% above the price.
The price implies 5.7% annual cash-flow growth, 4pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 9.2% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.24).
It runs a 19% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.99x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.7% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.9x net debt to EBITDA ($772.0M of cash against $2.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.7x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.1% over 3 years, 12.0% over 5 years and -1.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 20%).
At current returns, reinvesting 70% of profits supports about 12.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 14%.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (2.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.8%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.6% (0.9% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
The share count has grown 10.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years, raising it 39.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 10,700 employees, each generates about $507K of revenue, 1.4x the Industrials median.
That works out to $30K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
